title: April Fools That Fooled Millions
description: Spaghetti trees on the BBC, a 168 mph pitcher who never was, and Taco Bell's Liberty Bell

concepts.title: The Swiss Spaghetti Harvest
concepts.contentHtml:
On 1 April 1957, viewers of Panorama, the BBC's serious current-affairs program, watched a family in Ticino, in southern Switzerland, bring in their spaghetti harvest. Women plucked strands of spaghetti from the trees and laid them in the sun to dry. The narrator, Richard Dimbleby, explained that frost at the end of March could spoil the flavor, and that generations of growers had worked to make every strand grow to the same length.1

This year's crop was a bumper one, he said, thanks to a mild winter and the "virtual disappearance of the spaghetti weevil." The three-minute film had been shot at Morcote, on Lake Lugano, after the crew spent hours hanging spaghetti on the branches. An estimated eight million people watched, and hundreds rang the BBC to ask how to grow a spaghetti tree of their own. The BBC is said to have replied: "Place a sprig of spaghetti in a tin of tomato sauce and hope for the best."2

Even the BBC's own director-general, Sir Ian Jacob, was taken in.3 Part of the trick was the subject: in 1957 most Britons had only eaten spaghetti out of a tin and had no idea how it was made. Part was the messenger. Dimbleby, said the producer David Wheeler, "had enough gravitas to float an aircraft carrier." Wheeler never regretted the joke. He thought it was good for viewers to learn that "they couldn't believe everything they saw on the television."4

The film is believed to be one of the first April Fool's hoaxes ever staged on television.5 It showed what the new medium could do: moving pictures, a serious program and a trusted voice can make almost anything look like fact.

concepts.title: Sidd Finch, the 168 mph Rookie
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1 April 1985 issue of Sports Illustrated carried a startling scoop by George Plimpton. At their spring-training camp in St. Petersburg, Florida, the New York Mets were secretly trying out a "somewhat eccentric mystic" named Hayden (Sidd) Finch, who had no baseball career at all. When the pitching coach pointed a radar gun at Finch's fastball, the display read 168 mph. The story was crowded with real names, from the Mets' coaches and catchers to the commissioner of baseball, who was quoted saying: "I'll have to see it to believe it!"1

Finch, the story went, had briefly attended Harvard, learned his art in Tibet, played the French horn, and pitched with one foot bare and the other in a hiking boot. He had not decided between baseball and the horn, and would tell the Mets on April 1.2 For scale, the fastest pitch ever measured is 105.8 mph, thrown by Aroldis Chapman in 2010.3

The trick was to wrap one impossible number in layers of real, checkable detail. A few Mets officials were in on it: they gave Joe Berton, a 6-foot-4 Chicago middle-school teacher, a uniform and the run of their camp, so he could be photographed as Finch.4 And Plimpton hid a confession in plain sight. The subhead began "He's a pitcher, part yogi and part recluse. Impressively liberated from our opulent life-style, Sidd's deciding about yoga" and ended "and his future in baseball." The first letters spell HAPPY APRIL FOOLS DAY, AH FIB. Fans, and even other journalists, believed it anyway, and the magazine owned up only on April 15.5

concepts.title: Taco Bell Buys the Liberty Bell
concepts.contentHtml:
On 1 April 1996, readers of six big American newspapers, among them the New York Times, the Washington Post and USA Today, found a full-page ad headlined "Taco Bell Buys The Liberty Bell." In an effort to help the national debt, the fast-food chain announced, it had agreed to purchase the bell, which would now be called the "Taco Liberty Bell." A press release added that the bell would split its time between Philadelphia and the company's headquarters in Irvine, California, and compared the deal to companies adopting highways.1

Not everyone checked the date. The National Park Service, which looks after the bell, fielded hundreds of calls from furious Americans. Its director, Roger Kennedy, assured everyone that the ad was "as false as it is cheesy."2

Others played along. At the White House, press secretary Mike McCurry deadpanned that Ford was planning to refurbish the Lincoln Memorial: "It'll be the Lincoln Mercury Memorial." At 11 a.m. Taco Bell owned up, and it gave $50,000 for the bell's upkeep. Its sales reportedly jumped by $1 million over the next two days. David Paine, whose PR firm helped dream up the stunt, said the timing was perfect: companies were just starting to put their names on stadiums, so a sponsored Liberty Bell sounded like only one step further. Looking back, he called it "the original fake news."3

title: Broadcasts Gone Strange
description: A masked TV hijacker in Chicago, the day the BBC had no news, and Captain Midnight's HBO raid

concepts.title: The Max Headroom Hijacking
concepts.contentHtml:
On a Sunday night in Chicago, 22 November 1987, WGN-TV was showing Bears highlights on its 9 p.m. news when, at 9:14, the picture changed. A figure in a Max Headroom mask and a yellow blazer rocked from side to side in front of a whirring metal background, saying nothing, for about 25 seconds. When the sports came back, anchor Dan Roan said: "Well if you're wondering what just happened, so am I."1

Max Headroom was a cult TV character, billed as the first computer-generated TV host. He was really the comedian Matt Frewer in makeup and prosthetics, and in his own series he made a habit of hacking into the network's feed.2

Later that night the mask was back, this time on WTTW, Chicago's public TV station, in the middle of a Doctor Who rerun. Now there was garbled audio, and toward the end the intruder bared his bottom to an accomplice, who spanked him with a fly swatter. Staff in WTTW's master control could do nothing; after 90 seconds the pirate signal vanished on its own. The Federal Communications Commission investigated, but never worked out who was behind it.3

How was it done? The stations sent their programs by microwave from their studios to downtown skyscrapers, where they were rebroadcast across the city. An analog receiver has no way to check where a signal comes from. As Michael Marcus, the FCC official who wrote up the case for the FBI, later put it, the culprit probably "got close to the receiving end and just transmitted a signal that was received with a stronger strength than the more distant, intended signal." WGN broke free by switching its link to the Hancock building to a new frequency.4 To this day, the pirates remain unknown.5

concepts.title: The Day There Was No News
concepts.contentHtml:
On 18 April 1930, people across Britain tuned in to the BBC's 8:45 p.m. news bulletin and heard: "Good evening. Today is Good Friday. There is no news." For the rest of the 15-minute slot, the BBC played piano music.1 Then it went over to the Queen's Hall in London for a performance of Wagner's opera Parsifal.2

Accounts of the exact words vary; one has the announcer say "there is no news tonight." What is clear is that plenty had happened: one British newspaper gleefully pointed out a notable death, a fire and a car accident. The silence came from the BBC itself. In 1930 it had only a rudimentary news service and no separate news department. Newspapers, worried that radio news would eat into their sales, had worked to keep it small: before 1927 the BBC could not broadcast news before 7 p.m., and in 1930 its news staff was two editors and two sub-editors, who built bulletins from news agency reports arriving by teletype. Paid for by license fees rather than advertisers, it set a high bar for what counted as news, and later boasted that not broadcasting the news showed the merits of its service.3

The odd bulletin shows something easy to forget: the news is not a fixed quantity of events. It is a selection, and the amount depends on who is choosing, how many people they have, and who pays. A small BBC with four news staff and no ratings to chase could say there was nothing worth reporting. A modern 24-hour channel never would.

concepts.title: Captain Midnight Takes Over HBO
concepts.contentHtml:
Around midnight on 27 April 1986, viewers across the eastern two-thirds of the United States sat down to watch HBO's showing of The Falcon and the Snowman. Instead they got a row of color bars and a message: "Good Evening HBO from Captain Midnight, $12.95/month? No Way! Showtime/Movie Channel Beware!" It stayed on screen for four and a half minutes. The target was HBO's new scrambling of its satellite signal. People who had paid heavily for backyard dishes now found they could not watch it, and HBO offered descrambling equipment for $12.95 a month.1

Captain Midnight was John MacDougall, who ran a satellite-dish business in Ocala, Florida. Sales had collapsed, so he took a second job at Central Florida Teleport, an uplink station. Alone on the night shift, he swung its 30-foot dish toward Galaxy 1, the satellite carrying HBO, and sent up his own picture. It became a contest of sheer power. According to one account, HBO's operators on Long Island turned up their signal to fight back, then gave up for fear of damaging the satellite. Investigators reasoned that only a big professional uplink could have won. Of about 2,000 such facilities, 580 had a large enough antenna, and fewer than 100 used the typeface seen on screen.2

MacDougall pleaded guilty to transmitting without a radio license, paid a $5,000 fine and served a year's probation. The charge was awkward, since he actually held a license to transmit, and Congress then passed a law making satellite jamming a felony.3 Captain Midnight and the Max Headroom pirate used the same weakness: in analog broadcasting, the receiver obeys whichever signal arrives strongest.

title: Headlines That Were Wrong
description: Dewey Defeats Truman, Twain's real line on his own death, and Nobel's missing obituary

concepts.title: Dewey Defeats Truman
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous photograph of the 1948 American election shows the winner, Harry Truman, beaming as he holds up a newspaper that says he lost. Its banner reads DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN. The picture was taken two days after the vote, in St. Louis, as Truman headed back to Washington: Life photographer W. Eugene Smith caught the moment after a staffer handed him an early edition of the Chicago Daily Tribune.1

How did a big-city paper get it so wrong? Part of the answer is a labor dispute. The Tribune's union typesetters were on strike, so its front-page text was typed, cut and pasted, then photographed for the press.2

The other part is expectation. The Gallup organization predicted that Dewey would win comfortably, an error George Gallup put down to ending its polling three weeks before the election.3 Any late shift in opinion simply went unmeasured.

On election night the strike meant the Tribune had to choose its headline much earlier than usual. With few returns in, the editors trusted the judgment of their veteran reporter Arthur Sears Henning that Dewey had won. Within hours the count looked far closer. The next edition's banner was changed, and trucks scrambled to retrieve the 150,000 early copies.4

Truman won by 24,105,812 popular votes to Dewey's 21,970,065.5 The headline was a forecast printed as a fact, and an early deadline left no time to check it against the count.

concepts.title: The Report of My Death
concepts.contentHtml:
In the spring of 1897 Mark Twain had gone quiet. He and his wife had taken a rented house in Tedworth Square, London, where he was grieving for their daughter Susy, who had died the previous August, and writing the book that became Following the Equator.1 Silence breeds rumors. On 1 June several American papers, crediting the New York Herald, reported that he was "grievously ill and possibly dying", his intellect "shattered", and that he badly needed money.2

Reporters hurried to find him, and on 2 June the New York Journal printed his answer in a story by its reporter Frank Marshall White.3 It had all been a mix-up, Twain explained: his cousin James Ross Clemens had been seriously ill in London a few weeks earlier, and "the report of my illness grew out of his illness." Then came the line, in its original form: "The report of my death was an exaggeration."4

That is not the version most people quote. In the days and weeks that followed, newspapers retelling the story slipped in "greatly" or "grossly". Twain himself, recalling it in 1906, gave it as "Say the report is exaggerated." His biographer Albert Bigelow Paine, writing in 1912, polished it into "Just say the report of my death has been grossly exaggerated."5

Each retelling made the joke a little neater, and the neatest version won. A famous quotation is often the last draft of a story rather than the first.

concepts.title: The Obituary Nobody Can Find
concepts.contentHtml:
It is one of the best-loved stories in science. In 1888 Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite, opens a French newspaper and finds his own obituary under the headline "The merchant of death is dead." Horrified at how he will be remembered, he decides to leave his fortune to prizes for the good of humanity.

Part of it is solid. His brother Ludvig did die while staying in Cannes in 1888. Britannica still calls a newspaper mix-up the most plausible trigger for the prizes, while admitting that Nobel confided in no one about his decision and that "we can only speculate".1

The obituary itself is another matter. The paper usually named, Ideotie Quotidienne, basically exists only inside this tale, every telling leans on the same two quotations, and searches of books and news archives turn up nothing new.2 A 2024 paper in Substantia, a journal of the history of chemistry, found no record of that paper (the name translates as something like "Daily Nonsense"). It points instead to a premature notice in Le Figaro that was far too mild to have shaken Nobel, and concludes that the famous version is most likely made up.3

What the record does show is a man who thought about war and peace for years. He signed his last will in Paris on 27 November 1895, leaving much of his wealth to found the prizes.4 For the peace prize, many give the credit to his friend Bertha von Suttner, a leader of the peace movement who corresponded with him for years; the Nobel Prize's own site says there is little doubt the friendship shaped his will.5 The merchant-of-death story survives because it is a perfect parable, and parables travel better than footnotes.

title: Satire Taken Seriously
description: Swift's Modest Proposal, the Alternative 3 Mars hoax, and Onion spoofs reported as news

concepts.title: Swift's Modest Proposal
concepts.contentHtml:
The title promises something sensible: A Modest Proposal for preventing the children of poor people in Ireland from being a burden on their parents or country. The narrator sounds like a careful policy expert, armed with costs and head counts. Then he gets to the point. He has been assured, he says, that "a young healthy child well nursed, is, at a year old, a most delicious nourishing and wholesome food, whether stewed, roasted, baked, or boiled".1 The babies of the poor, in other words, should be raised as food.

The author was Jonathan Swift, dean of St Patrick's Cathedral, and his monstrous scheme was aimed at a real catastrophe. Ireland reached a crisis point in 1729: crop failures, high unemployment, rising prices and trade restrictions imposed by the British government had left thousands in homelessness and poverty, and Swift had watched the famine's toll on the poor at first hand.2

The sharpest move comes near the end. "Let no man talk to me of other expedients," the narrator says, and then lists them anyway: taxing absentees, and using no clothes or furniture "except what is of our own growth and manufacture".3 These were Swift's true proposals, disguised as solutions his narrator would never consider.4 The horror is a frame; the serious program is hidden inside it.

Did readers fall for it? The reaction suggests not. The pamphlet was well received and reprinted several times in London and Dublin within months, and though it carried no name, the identity of the author was well known.5 Its method is still the model for deadpan satire: a monstrous idea argued in a perfectly reasonable voice.

concepts.title: Alternative 3: Escape to Mars
concepts.contentHtml:
On 20 June 1977, viewers of ITV's Science Report were told that a planned film about Britain's brain drain had gone badly wrong. Scientists the team had tried to interview were not just leaving the country; they seemed to be disappearing from the face of the Earth.1

What followed was Alternative 3, an April Fool's hoax that had been delayed by almost three months. Fronted by the newsreader Tim Brinton, it claimed that Earth was heading for environmental collapse and that NASA's Moon flights were secretly preparing an escape to Mars for a chosen elite, with most of humanity left to die. It even showed "secret" footage of a 1962 Mars landing finding signs of life, faked on a budget by the director's fingers wriggling under red sand.2

The clues were in plain sight. The closing credits said the characters were played by actors and gave the date as 1 April 1977, yet many viewers were taken in. ITV and Anglia revealed the hoax an hour after it ended, but newspapers kept up a show of outrage for weeks, and the program has never been repeated on British television.3

For some, the reveal was the cover-up. A few viewers refused to believe it was a joke even after the producers said so, and insist that the hoax label is part of a vast disinformation scheme.4 When a book version by Leslie Watkins appeared in 1978, tales spread that the first print run had been pulped on government orders and that secret agents had bought up the unsold copies; none of it was true.5 The show worked because it borrowed every signal of a real documentary: a trusted series title, a familiar news face, a sober tone. Viewers trusted the form before they weighed the content.

concepts.title: When The Onion Became News
concepts.contentHtml:
In November 2012 the satirical paper The Onion named North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-un, its "Sexiest Man Alive". China's People's Daily Online took it straight. Under the headline "North Korea's top leader named The Onion's Sexiest Man Alive for 2012", it ran a 55-image photo gallery of Kim, and removed it once it realized it had been duped.1

Two months earlier, Iran's Fars News Agency had picked up an Onion report that "according to the results of a Gallup poll released Monday, the overwhelming majority of rural white Americans said they would rather vote for Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad than U.S. president Barack Obama."2 There was no such poll. The Fars story was copied almost word for word from The Onion.3

Why does satire fool professional newsrooms? Satirical sites copy the tone and look of real news, so spotting the joke depends on context: you have to know the issue, know what normal political talk sounds like and recognize exaggeration.4 Lifted onto another site, a story loses most of that context: the masthead, the absurd headlines beside it, the reputation of the source. What remains reads like any other wire report.

The fix can be simple. Communication researchers who tested different warnings on social media posts found that labeling a story as satire worked unusually well: readers were less likely to believe it or share it, and they valued the warning.5
